Not really. Among other things, power conservation is going to be increasingly important.

Plus, there's also parallel processing, but writing parallel programs is really freaking hard and you can only go so far with it. Further, a lot of problems don't lend themselves well to parallel problem solving, and most of those only have certain parts that can benefit from it. With the way modern OS's are, there are a few ways you can get around this, e.g. split up a game into several different threads, and for some applications you can get a lot out of it, but ultimately it has some pretty important limitations. But it does have the benefit of being able to install more than one processor module on the motherboard, as opposed to cramming as many cores as possible on a single die.

There is also the possibility of specialized subprocessors. For instance, GPUs can be hooked together to make do-it-yourself supercomputer clusters, but they're crappy for regular programs. Get an array of specialized processors together and you might get an appreciable performance boost, at least for certain processing-intensive applications.

I suppose also that more usable transistor space could be recouped with at least one pretty fundamental change to the architecture. On an x86 chip, the system does not actually run the program code it is fed. The CISC code that humans write for it is rewritten into a more modern RISC code that is used by the real processor internally. Removing that translation layer could yield more usable space. However, one of Intel's greatest draws is backwards compatibility. There are ways to address this, e.g. emulation, JIT recompiling (which would basically move the translation layer from hardware to software) and other strategies. But that would be a very tough sell - Intel's tried it before, as has a company called Transmeta, but ultimately, the guarantees of "we promise, it's usually almost as fast as a real x86!" have been met with deafening silence and lost money.

The issue isn't that they can't make bigger chips, it's that they can't keep fitting more and more transistors into the same area. The cost of integrated circuits is generally per-area (more or less) instead of per-transistor which means the cost per transistor is going to stay pretty similar to what it is now (or even what it was a few years ago). This is why all the buzz in the last few years has been about more cores, GPU processing etc. instead of pumping up clock speeds and single-core performance.

They can definitely work on optimizing existing CPU designs to get more performance out of the same area of transistor, or they can just make things more and more parallel (again, GPUs are great for this because they're basically a giant grid of small cheap CPUs hooked up together). There's still a huge amount of progress to be made even if we can't keep shrinking things, but the time of "everything automatically doubles in computing power every two years" is over.
